title: Pontius Pilate
notes: Cited for: Pilate as Roman prefect of Judaea, 26 to 36 CE, who presided at Jesus's final trial and ordered his crucifixion.

title: Tacitus, Annals, Book 15 (Loeb Classical Library translation, 1937), on LacusCurtius
notes: Cited for: Annals 15.44, Christus put to death in the reign of Tiberius by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilate; 'the pernicious superstition'.

title: Amanda Witmer, 'Jesus was not a Christian and why it matters' (2013)
publisher: The Bible and Interpretation (University of Arizona)
notes: Cited for: the founder of what became Christianity was not a Christian but a Jew, an itinerant prophet, teacher and healer in Galilee.

title: New Testament
notes: Cited for: 27 books (Gospels, Acts, Epistles, Revelation); Paul's letters considered the earliest texts; written to bear witness to a faith.

title: Biblical literature: Determination of the canon in the 4th century
notes: Cited for: the canon of 27 New Testament books appears for the first time in the 39th Festal Letter of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in 367.

title: 367 Athanasius Defines the New Testament
notes: Cited for: Athanasius wrote his 367 list to end disputes over texts such as the Shepherd of Hermas and the Epistle of Barnabas.

title: From Jesus to Christ: The Importance of the Oral Tradition
notes: Cited for: Jesus died around 30; for 40 years there was no written gospel, and his followers passed on his story orally.

title: From Jesus to Christ: The Gospel of Mark
notes: Cited for: Mark as the first written gospel, around 70, drawing on earlier oral tradition; Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source.

title: Gospel (New Testament)
notes: Cited for: gospel from Anglo-Saxon god-spell, translating Greek euangelion, 'good news'; Mark generally considered earliest.

title: Trinity (Christianity)
notes: Cited for: the Trinity as the unity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit as three persons in one Godhead; not explicit in the New Testament; its form settled by the end of the 4th century; homoousios at Nicaea.

title: Nicene Creed
notes: Cited for: the only ecumenical creed, accepted by Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican and major Protestant churches; Constantinople 381; the filioque added in the West from the 6th century and rejected in the East.

title: Creed
notes: Cited for: a creed as an authoritative formulation of a religious community's beliefs, a brief affirmation used in worship.

title: Baptism
notes: Cited for: baptism as the sacrament of admission with water and the Trinitarian formula; immersion, pouring or sprinkling; Paul's image of sharing Christ's death and Resurrection; infant baptism in most traditional churches, believer's baptism among Baptists, rooted in the Anabaptists.

title: Eucharist
notes: Cited for: the Eucharist ('thanksgiving') commemorating the Last Supper, central act of worship; Catholic transubstantiation; Orthodox real presence; Lutheran, Zwinglian and Calvinist views; ordinance rather than sacrament.

title: Easter (holiday)
notes: Cited for: Easter celebrates the Resurrection on the third day after the Crucifixion; first Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox (March 21), between March 22 and April 25; Eastern Orthodox reckoning by the Julian calendar.

title: When is Easter?
notes: Cited for: Easter is the first Sunday after the full moon on or after the spring equinox, falling between 22 March and 25 April.

title: Church year
notes: Cited for: the church year's Christmas cycle (Advent, Christmas, Epiphany) and Easter cycle (Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Pentecost); Christmas on December 25; Sunday as the Lord's day; the 50 days from Easter to Pentecost.

title: Lent
notes: Cited for: Lent as a 40-day penitential preparation for Easter recalling Jesus's fast in the wilderness; Ash Wednesday in the West, Clean Monday in the East; fasting, abstinence, almsgiving, giving up pleasures.

title: Roman Catholicism
notes: Cited for: about 1.3 billion members, the largest Christian church; Catholic teaching that St. Peter was the first pope; apostolic succession through bishops; the seven sacraments.

title: Pope
notes: Cited for: the pope as bishop of Rome and successor of St. Peter in Catholic teaching, with full and supreme jurisdiction; election by cardinals under 80 in a conclave by a two-thirds majority.

title: Diocese
notes: Cited for: a diocese as a territory administered by a bishop and divided into parishes; in the Catholic Church only the pope creates, divides or merges dioceses.

title: Eastern Orthodoxy
notes: Cited for: autocephalous churches with the Ecumenical Patriarch's honorary primacy; the Russian church as by far the largest; adherents mainly in the Balkans, the Middle East and former Soviet countries; icons in worship and homes, not objects of worship; the Divine Liturgy; the 1054 schism.

title: Orthodox churches (Eastern)
notes: Cited for: autocephalous churches listed (Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, Russia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Georgia, Cyprus, Greece and others); the Ecumenical Patriarch as 'first among equals'; veneration of icons; services in national languages.

title: Martin Luther
notes: Cited for: the Ninety-five Theses of October 31, 1517 against indulgences; salvation as a gift received by faith, not earned by works; sola scriptura; the German Bible; the split of Western Christianity.

title: Diet of Worms
notes: Cited for: Leo X excommunicated Luther on January 3, 1521; at Worms in April 1521 Luther refused to recant unless shown wrong by Scripture or reason.

title: Martin Luther Might Not Have Nailed His 95 Theses to the Church Door (Becky Little)
notes: Cited for: Luther sent the theses to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz on October 31, 1517; the door story comes from Melanchthon after Luther's death; much recent scholarship doubts it.

title: Global Christianity: The Size and Distribution of the World's Christian Population
notes: Cited for: about two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe in 1910 and 26% in 2010; in 2010 about half of Christians were Catholic, 37% Protestant broadly defined, 12% Orthodox.

title: Global Christianity: Christian Movements and Denominations
notes: Cited for: pentecostal and charismatic Christians together about 27% of all Christians in 2010; pentecostals seek a post-conversion baptism of the Holy Spirit with gifts such as prophecy, healing and tongues.

title: Pentecostalism
notes: Cited for: the name from the Holy Spirit's descent on the first Christians at Pentecost (Acts); baptism with the Holy Spirit, usually with speaking in tongues; prophecy and healing; lay leadership.

title: Spirit and Power: A 10-Country Survey of Pentecostals
notes: Cited for: pentecostals and other renewalists believe God, acting through the Holy Spirit, plays a direct, active role in everyday life; gifts such as tongues, healing and prophesying.

title: Michael Harper, 'Releasing the Spirit: the Pentecostals' (Christian History, issue 9, 1984)
notes: Cited for: Pentecostals regarded evangelism as the task of all Christians and encouraged lay leadership early.
